title: The Effort Perception with AI Art
author: void--null
selftext:
I think there's something to be said about the reputation of AI art in games specifically. Even as someone who's really into AI across the board, I have a gut reaction when I spot it in a game, and I think the core issue is a perceived effort gap. AI art is generally high resolution, well proportioned, polished looking, and when the gameplay doesn't match that level of care, people feel cheated.

I think the solution is you either have to make your game match the quality your art is projecting, or match your art to the scope of what you're actually building. Like if I see a visual novel with gorgeous art but the story is half-baked, or a colony sim with really detailed sprites but the gameplay is just things walking around, it feels cheap. It's not that games have to be incredible before they're allowed to have good art, it's just that I need to be able to imagine you spent the same amount of time on both.

What do you guys think? I feel like it's a reasonable middle ground to still use the speedups that AI gives you without it making the overalll project feel cheaper.

Some will pick objectively "nicer" images, but the point holds, AI gen simply has no value in its core, and its bound to be generic, because its a simple mix of everything that ever existed visually. 

And also I have no idea why you push do hard into discussing how exploitative is the gamedev world. Some companies are crap, some are not. And now due to raise of AI the grind/exploatation is even worse, because now artists are forced to do much more work, for same/worse wages, while much less care goes into end product. replies.author: MysteriousPepper8908
replies.body:
Neural Viz and Aze Alter are both doing interesting things with AI, there's the artist Cuco and the team from Cal Art's that brought an AI-assisted short to Sundance, Eliza McNitt's Ancestral, all doing unique and interesting things with AI but since you're running on cognitive bias, you see any similarity to what has come before in AI as being derivative and the same thing in non-AI art as being inspired and there is no way to get past cognitive bias for someone who refuses to recognize it.


AI art is as with anything, subject to the style and interests of the person using it. No medium has inherent tastes or vision, that is for the person wielding it to decide and all of these creators have a unique vision and aesthetic. Perhaps not wholly unique from everything that has come before, nothing is, but something that expresses who they are and what they value 


Many large companies have rejected AI because they fear that smaller creators will be able to compete and sure, they can still choose to employ exploitative practices but as AI improves, artists are less reliant on them and their resources to realize their vision. Mainstream projects have by and large always been slop designed to appeal to the widest demographic with a handful of exceptions in a given year. Now, the floodgates are open to individuals realizing their visions unconstrained by needing to appeal to executives and shareholders to get their projects over the line.

replies.author: MysteriousPepper8908
replies.body:
Well, there are tools that aren't going anywhere because they're local but I don't necessarily expect you to have any regard for the AI aspect as a technical process. However, if you actually look into the process these creators use, AI is only a part of it. Cuco and the Cal Art's team used their own hand drawn designs as a basis for the AI, Neural Viz and Aze Alter use their own writing and voice acting so even if you don't care for the parts that are AI, that doesn't invalidate the effort put into the project as a whole.


No, that hasn't been proven at all, there has been a rejection of AI from production studios like 2K that want to dominate media with their middle of the road crap but if you're a skilled 3D artist, you're still not going to be able to make films and cinematics like the big guy's unless you have many millions in rendering hardware. CalArts is a prestigious school and those are skilled animators but if they wanted to do the same thing with s traditional workflow, they would need a team twice the size to do it. Neural Viz has an industry background but an entire production workflow at that level is traditionally impossible for one person. Many professionals are using these tools to extend their capabilities and that will only be more true over time.


Anything can look shallow if you lack the insight to understand it. d:

replies.author: LatentBlade
replies.body: "And they weren't sampling these records because they were too lazy to write their own music. They weren't sampling these records to cash in on the familiarity of the original stuff. To be honest, it was all about sampling really obscure things, except for a few obvious exceptions like Vanilla Ice and "doo doo doo da da doo doo" that we know about. But the thing is, they were sampling those records because they heard something in that music that spoke to them that they instantly wanted to inject themselves into the narrative of that music. They heard it, they wanted to be a part of it, and all of a sudden they found themselves in possession of the technology to do so, not much unlike the way the Delta blues struck a chord with the Stones and the Beatles and Clapton, and they felt the need to co-opt that music for the tools of their day. "

comments.author: Erandelax
comments.body:
*That* is not perceived as quality or "level of care", it is perceived as uncanny valley effect rampaging in full force. It would still remain off-putting for many people regardless of what gameplay is. The more perfect something attempts to look the more "that shit is unnatural" tags will get assigned to it by the brain. 

Having good gameplay would compensate it greatly through but not because of some "it's looks less cheap" considerations. It's just the very same flaws people nitpick and criticise down to the last digit in bad games get willingly brushed off and ignored in good ones. We tend to look more at good side of things we like and bad side of things we do not. 

Unless art is the central figure of your game... make a good game and you can replace all the art with pixelated stickmen and kid drawings and it still would work fine, make a bad game and regardless what art you pack into it, it will be beyond saving.
